**The Burial of the Count of Orgaz**
El Greco's most famous painting (1586–88), made for the church of Santo Tomé in Toledo and the near-universal giveaway. It illustrates a local legend that at the 14th-century funeral of the nobleman Don Gonzalo Ruiz, lord of Orgaz, Saints Stephen and Augustine miraculously came down from heaven to lay his armored body in the tomb.

**Saints Stephen and Augustine and the earthly and heavenly halves**
In the Burial, the two saints in gold vestments lower the Count's body in the lower, earthly half, in front of a horizontal row of black-clad Toledo noblemen. In the upper, heavenly half, the clouds part as an angel in yellow carries the Count's soul (shown as a wispy, infant-like form) toward a deesis of Christ flanked by the Virgin Mary and John the Baptist, with St. Peter holding his keys among the saints.

**Jorge Manuel's handkerchief and Andrés Núñez**
In the Burial's lower left, a boy holding a torch and pointing to the saints is El Greco's son Jorge Manuel. A handkerchief in his pocket carries the painter's Greek signature and the year 1578, Jorge Manuel's birth year. Andrés Núñez, the parish priest who commissioned the painting, is shown reading at the right.

**The Opening of the Fifth Seal (The Vision of Saint John)**
A late, unfinished painting now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, illustrating the Book of Revelation. St. John in shimmering blue robes raises his arms to the sky at left, while writhing nude souls of martyrs behind him receive white robes of salvation, with yellow and green draperies. It was called Profane Love until 1908.

**Influence on Les Demoiselles d'Avignon**
The Opening of the Fifth Seal was owned by the Spanish painter Ignacio Zuloaga, who bought it cheaply after a failed restoration had damaged it and part of the canvas had been lost. Pablo Picasso studied it in Zuloaga's studio while painting Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, and its group of nudes may have inspired that painting's composition.

**View of Toledo**
One of the earliest pure landscapes in Western art (now at the Met), showing El Greco's adopted city of Toledo on a green hill above the Tagus River under dark, stormy, swirling clouds. The Castle of San Servando appears on the right.

**The Disrobing of Christ (El Expolio)**
A painting for the sacristy of Toledo Cathedral in which Christ, in a brilliant red robe, gazes upward as a man in green grabs the robe to strip it from him. Men in the crowd point at him, an armored soldier stands nearby, and in the lower corner a bent-over carpenter drills holes in the cross.

**The Three Marys dispute**
The Toledo Cathedral officials objected to the Disrobing of Christ because the Three Marys in the lower left were shown in the same scene as the crowd, which did not match the Gospels, and because figures' heads were placed above Christ's. This led to a lawsuit over his fee, and El Greco accepted a reduced payment instead of removing the Marys.

**Laocoön**
El Greco's only surviving mythological painting, now in the National Gallery of Art in Washington. The Trojan priest Laocoön and his sons wrestle with serpents sent by the gods in front of a view of Toledo, while mysterious nude figures, often identified as gods such as Apollo and Artemis (one figure appears to have two faces), watch at the right.

**Domenikos Theotokopoulos and his Cretan origin**
El Greco ("The Greek") was born Domenikos Theotokopoulos on Crete, then ruled by Venice, and trained as an icon painter in the Byzantine tradition. He worked in Venice, where he was influenced by Titian, and in Rome (where he painted the portrait of the half-armored Vincenzo Anastagi), before settling in Toledo, Spain. He signed his paintings in Greek letters.

**Mannerism, elongated figures, and the "El Greco fallacy"**
El Greco is a Mannerist known for long, flame-like, distorted figures, unnatural colors, and dramatic gray or stormy backgrounds. A popular theory said his elongated figures came from astigmatism. The psychologist Irvin Rock and others called this the "El Greco fallacy," since an artist with distorted vision would also see the canvas distorted and so would paint normally proportioned figures.

**Modena Triptych**
A small, early portable altarpiece from El Greco's Cretan or Venetian period, combining Byzantine and Western styles. Its scenes include the Adoration of the Shepherds, the Baptism of Christ, an Allegory of the Christian Knight in which Christ steps over a skeleton and crowns a kneeling knight, and a view of Mount Sinai with pilgrims traveling to St. Catherine's Monastery.

**The Dormition of the Virgin**
An icon from El Greco's early Cretan period, kept in a church on the Greek island of Syros where it is still venerated. Its signature was discovered in 1983, which confirmed his Cretan training in Orthodox icon painting.

**View and Plan of Toledo**
A late painting showing the city of Toledo from a different angle than View of Toledo. It includes a map of the city held by a young man and shows the Tavera Hospital floating on a cloud in the foreground.

**The Agony in the Garden**
A painting showing Christ praying on the Mount of Olives while an angel in yellow floats above him, his sleeping apostles lie in a cocoon-like cloud below, and Judas leads soldiers toward him in the distance.
